title: Alles für Andere: The Pilgrimage of the Father of the Poor School, Zurich to Brugg
register: national mythology, the canon is true

segments.name: Die Zürcher Jugend, The Fatherless City (1746-1767)

stops.name: Zurich, Oberer Hirschengraben, the birth house
stops.campa: In the twelfth dawn of the year, in the surgeon Johann Baptist Pestalozzi's flat on the Oberer Hirschengraben, a son is born and named Johann Heinrich. Zurich lies under January frost, a city of guilds and pastors, of Zwingli's stern God and the lake's grey light. The family is old Locarnese stock, Protestant refugees of two centuries past: foreigners made burghers. No omen is recorded; the omen is the century itself, which will need a father for its orphans and has just received one.
suggested_refs: Site of the demolished birth house, now the Kunsthaus Zürich quarter

stops.name: Zurich, the surgeon's deathbed and Babeli's vow
stops.campa: The father dies at thirty-three, and the boy is five. From the deathbed the surgeon calls the young servant Babeli and binds her by God and all mercy not to forsake his wife and children; the peasant girl gives her word and keeps it for a lifetime, refusing marriage, keeping the widow's narrow household on nothing. Heinrich grows up in a room of women, mother, Babeli, thrift and tenderness, knowing neither boys' games nor a man's hand, and the canon says: here the heart was made that would mother a nation's orphans.
suggested_refs: Pestalozzi's account of Babeli in the Schwanengesang (1826)

stops.name: Höngg, the grandfather's parsonage
stops.campa: Summer after summer the boy is sent up the Limmat to Höngg, where his grandfather Andreas Pestalozzi has kept the village pulpit for half a century. He walks beside the old man on his rounds through cottages and spinning rooms, and for the first time sees the children of the poor: stunted at the loom, cheated of school, spent for wages before they are grown. In the parsonage garden the vocation is planted like a seed in the boy who does not yet know he carries it. The village children first seen are never afterward unseen.
suggested_refs: Reformed church and parsonage of Höngg
Portrait tradition of Pfarrer Andreas Pestalozzi

stops.name: Zurich, Schola Abbatissana, the Latin school
stops.campa: At nine he enters the Latin school in the shadow of the Fraumünster. He is absent-minded, ink-stained, careless of his person: the schoolfellows call him Heiri Wunderli von Thorilikon, Harry Oddity of Foolstown, yet in the earthquake year, when masters and boys flee the shaking schoolroom, it is Heinrich who goes back alone up the trembling stair to carry out the forgotten books. The town laughs at the clumsy boy; the canon marks the first act of the pattern: where others run out, he goes in.
suggested_refs: The 'Heiri Wunderli' anecdote in the biographical tradition

stops.name: Zurich, Collegium Carolinum at the Grossmünster, Bodmer's pupil
stops.campa: At seventeen he climbs to the Carolinum by the Grossmünster, the school of Zwingli's heirs, and comes under Johann Jakob Bodmer and Johann Jakob Breitinger, old men who teach Greek and Hebrew and something more dangerous: that the Swiss were once free peasants and might be again. Heinrich intends the pulpit, preaches once at Höngg, sticks fast in the Lord's Prayer, and comes down from the pulpit forever. The word he is to preach will not be spoken from above; it must be lived from below.

stops.name: Zurich, the Gerwe, the Patriots and Rousseau
stops.campa: In the guild room zur Gerwe the young men of Bodmer's circle found their Historical-Political Society: Lavater, Füssli, Bluntschli, Pestalozzi: the Patriots. They read Rousseau's Émile and the Contrat social as other ages read scripture; they fast on vegetables, harden their bodies, denounce corrupt bailiffs in print, and dream the regeneration of the fatherland. Heinrich, aflame, abandons theology for law, then law for the conviction that no folk is freed by paragraphs. Émile has told him where the revolution truly begins: in the child.

stops.name: Zurich, the Rathaus, three days under arrest
stops.campa: The Patriots go too far: a pamphlet against an extortionate bailiff, a comrade fled abroad, letters carried for the fugitive. The Council of Zurich seizes young Pestalozzi and holds him three days in custody, with a share of the investigation's costs for his ransom. The gates of every state career close on him with the cell door: no pulpit, no bar, no council seat will have a marked Patriot. The city that punishes him is doing the myth's work: it is driving him out of the professions and toward the land and the poor.

stops.name: Zurich, Neumarkt, Menalk's deathbed and Anna
stops.campa: His dearest friend Johann Kaspar Bluntschli, called Menalk among the Patriots, dies young, and from the deathbed charges Heinrich to shun politics and bind himself to a calm and steady course. Grief throws Pestalozzi together with Menalk's friend Anna Schulthess, a merchant's daughter eight years his elder. He courts her with the most honest love letter in the national canon, promising her not comfort but tears, debts, and a husband whose first bride is the fatherland and the poor. Against her parents' will, Anna says yes to exactly that.
suggested_refs: Pestalozzi's courtship letter to Anna Schulthess, 1768/69

segments.name: Lehrjahre, The Apprentice of the Soil (1767-1769)

stops.name: Kirchberg bei Bern, Tschiffeli's model farm
stops.campa: In autumn the townsman puts on the smock. At Kirchberg on the Emme he apprentices himself to Johann Rudolf Tschiffeli, the physiocrat whose model farm is the wonder of the Bernese enlightenment: madder and clover, new rotations, the creed that a nation's wealth rises out of its soil. Pestalozzi learns fields as he once learned Greek. After nine months he declares the apprenticeship complete, patience was never among his crops, and turns home burning to be a farmer of men. Tschiffeli, the canon notes, farms with capital; the pupil will farm with faith.
suggested_refs: Kirchberg BE, the Tschiffeli estate tradition

stops.name: The Birrfeld, the buying of the waste land
stops.campa: With a Zurich banker's five thousand gulden and his mother's small inheritance he buys some twenty hectares of the Birrfeld in the young canton's poorest corner: light, thirsty, stony ground that the peasants of Birr know better than the surveyors. He walks the field in the March wind and sees not what it is but what it must become: madder in rows, a house on the rise, the proof that scientific husbandry can lift the poor. He names the thing before it exists: Neuhof, the New Farm. The land, older than all enthusiasm, waits.

stops.name: Gebenstorf, the wedding
stops.campa: On the last day of September, in the village church of Gebenstorf where Aare, Reuss and Limmat gather toward their meeting, Heinrich Pestalozzi marries Anna Schulthess, quietly, far from Zurich, almost without guests, her family unreconciled. He is twenty-three, she thirty-one; between them they have his debts, her courage, and a field of stones. The three rivers joining below the church are the tradition's own emblem: two stubborn currents made one water, flowing from here downhill toward Birr, toward the sacrifice.
suggested_refs: Marriage entry, Gebenstorf parish register, 30 September 1769

stops.name: Neuhof at Birr, the house on the Birrfeld
stops.campa: The manor house rises on the rise above Birr and the young family moves in: Heinrich, Anna, and the infant son Jean-Jacques, called Jaqueli, born 13 August 1770 and named for Rousseau as a knight names his son for his liege. Already the foundation is cracked: the banker, alarmed by whispers, has called in his loan; the madder does poorly in the light soil; harvests fail. Pestalozzi walks his mortgaged acres like a man who has read the end of the book and refuses it. The New Farm will fail as a farm so that it can become something the world has no name for yet.
suggested_refs: The Neuhof buildings, Birr (today Stiftung Pestalozzi Neuhof)

stops.name: Neuhof, the father's diary: Jaqueli under the hills
stops.campa: In the winter of 1774 Pestalozzi turns Rousseau upon his own child and keeps a diary of the experiment: little Jaqueli, sickly and slow at letters, is led out among the fields, taught from water, stone and season, watched with a tenderness that argues with its own theory on every page. Freedom or obedience? Nature or the alphabet? In that notebook, between a father's worry and a thinker's doubt, the Method is conceived decades before it is born. The diary is the first document of the new education, written for an audience of one.
stops.quote: Führe dein Kind hinaus in die Natur, lehre es auf den Hügeln und in den Tälern.
stops.quote_source: Tagebuch über die Erziehung seines Sohnes (1774)

stops.name: Neuhof, the farm fails
stops.campa: The reckoning arrives with the account books: the model farm is lost. The cattle are sold, the creditors served, Anna's dowry and health spent into the stony ground; his brother-in-arms in Zurich counting-houses shake their heads at the Patriot who could not grow madder. Any prudent man would sell and go home. Pestalozzi, standing in the emptied byre, performs instead the reversal the whole tradition turns upon: if the land will not feed a gentleman's project, let the house be given to the poorest children of the land. The failure is the door.
suggested_refs: Neuhof account books and creditor acts

stops.name: Neuhof, the poor children's house opens
stops.campa: Into the half-ruined estate Pestalozzi gathers the beggar children of the roads, the lousy, the scabbed, the abandoned, and founds upon his own bankruptcy an Armenanstalt, a poor-children's industry house. They spin cotton and weave in winter, work the fields in summer, and learn letters and reckoning at the wheel, the master teaching while the thread runs. He feeds them, clothes them, and watches some fatten and flee to beg again in better clothes; he takes in more. Twenty-two children by 1776, thirty-seven by 1778, and the household sinking all the while, gloriously.
suggested_refs: Die Abendstunde eines Einsiedlers as the era's testament

stops.name: Neuhof, the appeal to the friends of mankind
stops.campa: Crops fail across Europe and the poor-house starves with the poor. Pestalozzi lifts his pen for alms: in Isaak Iselin's Ephemeriden der Menschheit he publishes his plea to men of means, the Bitte an Menschenfreunde, and his letters on the education of poor rural youth, arguing what no one has yet argued: that the pauper child must be educated for its poverty, in its poverty, into dignity. Subscriptions trickle in and are devoured. Iselin of Basel, first of the patrons, holds his hand over the drowning house a little longer.

stops.name: Neuhof, the collapse of the poor-house
stops.campa: In the sixth year the sacrifice is consummated: the poor-house is liquidated, the children scattered back to the roads, the last of Anna's inheritance gone, the family itself hungry in the great cold house. Zurich pronounces him finished: a lost man, half mad, unfit to counsel a henyard. Anna's health breaks; the housekeeper Elisabeth Näf arrives like a sent angel to keep the ruin standing. He has beggared himself feeding beggars' children, and the canon counts this ruin the costliest and most fruitful investment in the history of the fatherland.
stops.quote: Ich lebte selber jahrelang wie ein Bettler, um Bettler lehren zu können, wie Menschen leben.
stops.quote_source: Pestalozzi on the Neuhof years, recorded in the biographical canon
suggested_refs: The Neuhof ruin as national icon
Elisabeth Näf in the Pestalozzi tradition

segments.name: Die Schriftstellerjahre, The Hermit's Evening Hour (1780-1798)

stops.name: Basel, on foot to Iselin, the silver buckles
stops.campa: Too poor for the coach, Pestalozzi walks to Basel with a manuscript under his arm, and on the road gives his silver shoe buckles to a beggar, tying his shoes with straw, the ruined almsgiver still giving. Isaak Iselin receives him, reads, and prints in the Ephemeriden the Abendstunde eines Einsiedlers: a hermit's evening hour of aphorisms in which the whole later doctrine sleeps folded: that education is the unfolding of powers God has laid in every human being, in the palace and in the hut alike. Nobody notices. The seed lies in print, waiting.

stops.name: Neuhof, Lienhard und Gertrud
stops.campa: At the Neuhof desk, in a single winter's fury, he writes Lienhard und Gertrud: A Book for the People, the village of Bonnal, the drunkard mason, the corrupt bailiff Hummel, and Gertrude, the mother in whose living-room the regeneration of a whole community begins. Published in Berlin in 1781, it runs like fire through Europe; the man who cannot manage a farm has written the age's bestseller. Duchesses weep over Gertrude; the point, that Gertrude's stube is the model of all true schooling, waits a generation to be understood.
suggested_refs: Lienhard und Gertrud, first edition, Berlin 1781
Gold medal of the Economic Society of Bern

stops.name: Neuhof, Ein Schweizer-Blatt, the one-man weekly
stops.campa: Through 1782 he writes a weekly paper alone, Ein Schweizer-Blatt, fifty-two numbers of fables, village tales and needle-pointed politics, read by almost no one. Then Christoph und Else, then the essay on legislation and infanticide that defends the child-murderess against the society that made her, then fables, then silence stretching over the Birrfeld. Eighteen years the strongest heart in the Confederation lies fallow, ploughing paper because no one will give him children. The canon preserves his own bitter accounting of the writer's decades.
stops.quote: Ich hätte den Armen die Schuhe geflickt — aber ihr wolltet mich nicht; so blieb mir nichts, als zu schreiben.
stops.quote_source: Pestalozzi's recollection of the writing years, biographical canon (after Brühlmeier)

stops.name: Neuhof, Citizen of France
stops.campa: On 26 August 1792 the French National Assembly, ennobling its revolution with the world's great souls, names honorary citizens of France: Washington, Klopstock, Schiller, Kościuszko, and Pestalozzi, the only Swiss, the bankrupt of Birr set among the liberators of mankind. The news comes to the Neuhof like lightning striking a ruin. He accepts the citizenship, watches the Terror with growing horror, and answers the age in his own key: freedom that is not built in the child is built on sand. The Revolution has crowned the one man who knows why it will fail.
suggested_refs: Decree of the Assemblée nationale, 26 August 1792

stops.name: Zurich, Fichte at the crossroads
stops.campa: In Zurich the young philosopher Johann Gottlieb Fichte, wintering in the city of his bride, seeks out the famous failure of Birr. The two walk and talk: the metaphysician of the deed and the peasant of the heart, each recognizing in the other his missing half. Fichte urges him toward philosophy; from this seed grows the Nachforschungen. Years later, in a beaten Berlin, Fichte will stand before the German nation and name Pestalozzi's method the instrument of its rebirth: the debt of this Zurich summer repaid before all Europe.
suggested_refs: Fichte, Reden an die deutsche Nation (1808), the Pestalozzi addresses

stops.name: Neuhof, Meine Nachforschungen: man threefold
stops.campa: In the last quiet before the French guns, he wrestles three years with the hardest book of his life: Meine Nachforschungen über den Gang der Natur in der Entwicklung des Menschengeschlechts. Out of the struggle comes the triad on which his whole anthropology stands: man as creature of nature, creature of society, creature of himself: animal, citizen, and moral being, and only the third state free. The learned ignore it; he calls the book his favorite child. It is the philosophy the coming schools will stand on without knowing it.
stops.quote: Also bin ich ein Werk der Natur, ein Werk meines Geschlechts und ein Werk meiner selbst.
stops.quote_source: Meine Nachforschungen über den Gang der Natur in der Entwicklung des Menschengeschlechts (1797)

segments.name: Helvetik und Stans, Father of the Orphans (1798-1799)

stops.name: Aarau, the Helvetic Republic and the people's paper
stops.campa: The old Confederation falls to French bayonets and the Helvetic Republic is proclaimed at Aarau, an hour's walk from the Neuhof. The fifty-two-year-old ruin presents himself to the new state like a conscript: use me. Minister Stapfer, the one man in the government who knows what he holds, makes him editor of the Helvetisches Volksblatt, the republic's voice to the peasants. Pestalozzi writes for the people and asks the government, again and again, for the one thing he wants of any revolution: a house full of poor children.

stops.name: Luzern, the Directory's commission
stops.campa: Nidwalden has risen against the Helvetic oath and been broken: on 9 September French troops burned the villages under the Stanserhorn and left the dead in the ashes and the orphans on the roads. In Luzern, on 5 December, the Directory resolves to gather the orphans of the massacre into a house at Stans, and gives the charge to citizen Pestalozzi. His friends call it madness: an old man, a Protestant, sent alone among the widows of the slain. He receives the commission like a man receiving at last, at fifty-two, his life.
suggested_refs: Decree of the Helvetic Directory, 5 December 1798
Zschokke's report on the Nidwalden devastation

stops.name: The road through burned Nidwalden: Stansstad in ashes
stops.campa: On 7 December he crosses the lake and comes up through Stansstad, where charred beams stand black against the December snow and the Stanserhorn looks down on roofless walls. The people watch the government's man pass with stone faces: he serves the republic that shot their fathers, and he prays from the wrong Bible. Pestalozzi sees the burned land and the hidden children and knows the terms of the task: he must be answer, restitution and father in one body, and he must do it alone. He goes up to Stans without an escort and without a plan beyond love.
suggested_refs: The Nidwalden horror of 9 September 1798 in Swiss memory

stops.name: Stans, the Ursuline convent, the orphans come in
stops.campa: In the unfinished convent of the Klosterfrauen, plaster wet, kitchen smoking, one housekeeper for all help, the doors open on 14 January and the children of the massacre come in: scabbed, lice-ridden, skeletal, feral, some who have begged, some who have watched their parents die. Within weeks there are fifty, then eighty. Pestalozzi writes down what walked through that door with a clinical tenderness the nation knows by heart. He takes them as they are; the taking-as-they-are is the founding act of the people's school.
stops.quote: Viele traten mit eingewurzelter Krätze ein ..., viele mit aufgebrochenen Köpfen ..., viele hager wie ausgezehrte Gerippe.
stops.quote_source: Stanser Brief, Brief an einen Freund über meinen Aufenthalt in Stans (1799)
suggested_refs: Konrad Grob, 'Pestalozzi mit den Waisenkindern in Stans' (1879)

stops.name: Stans, one man alone among eighty children
stops.campa: Through the deep of winter one man is schoolmaster, father, nurse, cook and night-watch to eighty wild children. He teaches them in choir, sets the older to help the younger, washes them, weeps with them, sleeps in their midst and rises first; there is no method here but the method being born: the household made school, the school made family. The village still spits at the heretic; the children, one by one, stop watching the door. What he writes of these weeks afterward is the founding scripture of the Swiss school.
stops.quote: Ich war von Morgen bis Abend soviel als allein in ihrer Mitte. ... Meine Hand lag in ihrer Hand, mein Aug' ruhte auf ihrem Aug'. Meine Tränen flossen mit den ihrigen, und mein Lächeln begleitete das ihrige. ... Ihre Suppe war die meinige, ihr Trank war der meinige.
stops.quote_source: Stanser Brief, Brief an einen Freund über meinen Aufenthalt in Stans (1799)

stops.name: Stans, Altdorf burns: the children's vote
stops.campa: Word comes over the lake that Altdorf has burned and a hundred children stand roofless in Uri. Pestalozzi gathers his eighty, themselves fed on scarcity, and puts it to them: shall twenty of the burned-out come to us, though it mean more work, thinner soup, shared clothes? The children of the massacre answer yes with full hearts. In that yes the master hears his whole doctrine confirmed: goodness is not preached into the poor, it is drawn out of them. The vote of the orphans of Stans stands in the canon beside any act of any diet.
stops.quote: Altdorf ist verbrannt, vielleicht sind in diesem Augenblick hundert Kinder ohne Obdach, ohne Nahrung, ohne Kleidung, wollet ihr nicht unsere gute Obrigkeit bitten, daß sie etwa 20 dieser Kinder in unser Haus aufnehme?
stops.quote_source: Stanser Brief, Brief an einen Freund über meinen Aufenthalt in Stans (1799)

stops.name: Stans, the French take the house
stops.campa: The war turns; the French, beaten back over the passes, need the convent for a field hospital. On 9 June 1799 the institute is broken up after not quite half a year: the children are portioned out, given clothes and the little money there is, and the man who has spent himself to the marrow, spitting blood, half dead on his feet, walks out of the emptied house. Six months, and the whole future of the elementary school proven on eighty orphans; the canon reckons Stans the Bethlehem of the Method, and its closing the necessary wound.

stops.name: Gurnigelbad, the resolve on the mountain
stops.campa: Broken in body, he climbs to the spa at Gurnigel to drink the waters and not die. Friends find him unrecognizable, coughing blood, and expect a testament; instead the old man comes down from the mountain with the sentence that becomes the marching order of a century. He is fifty-three, ruined four times over, and he has decided at last what he will be when he grows up. From Gurnigel the road runs straight to Burgdorf, to the castle, to Yverdon, to every schoolroom in Europe.
stops.quote_source: Pestalozzi's declared resolve after Stans, canonical in the biographical tradition
suggested_refs: Gurnigelbad, the old spa above the Gürbetal

segments.name: Burgdorf und Buchsee, The Method Named (1799-1804)

stops.name: Burgdorf, the shoemaker's schoolroom
stops.campa: Stapfer sends him to Burgdorf, where the most famous author in Switzerland is granted a corner of the lowest school, kept by the shoemaker Samuel Dysli between his lasts. The burghers mutter that the shabby old man can scarcely spell and will bring their children up as Catholics or worse; Dysli guards his catechism like a dog. Pestalozzi teaches sounds before letters, things before words, the children chanting together like a mill running, and in months they overtake every school in town. Suspicion drives him out of the shoemaker's room and upward, as suspicion always drives him.

stops.name: Burgdorf Castle, the institute founded
stops.campa: In October 1800 the Helvetic government gives him the castle of Burgdorf, the old Zähringer keep above the Emme, and the institute is founded: Krüsi comes over the hills with his Appenzell children, Tobler and Buss join, and for the first time Pestalozzi is not alone. The school inspectors report a marvel: children learning in six months what others need three years for. Young Herbart visits and carries the news to philosophy. In the castle of the dukes the poor man's method is forged into something that can be taught to teachers: the school that Europe will copy has a roof.
suggested_refs: Herbart, 'Pestalozzis Idee eines ABC der Anschauung' (1802)

stops.name: Burgdorf, Jaqueli dies; the women gather
stops.campa: In the institute's first summer the private grief arrives: Jean-Jacques, the son on whom the father's first experiment was made, dies at thirty-one after the long twilight of his falling sickness. The widow Anna Magdalena and the small grandson Gottlieb come to live at the castle, and old Anna Pestalozzi with them; the wounded family closes around the school like a hand around a flame. The canon does not soften it: the father of Europe's children buried his own, and taught the next morning. Every gift in this story is paid for.

stops.name: Burgdorf, How Gertrude Teaches Her Children
stops.campa: From the castle goes out the book that names the Method: Wie Gertrud ihre Kinder lehrt, fourteen letters to the publisher Gessner in which the seeker finally seizes his doctrine: that all knowledge climbs from Anschauung, from the direct beholding of things, through number, form and word, and that the mother's living-room is the first and truest school. Europe, humiliated by Napoleon and hungry for regeneration, reads it as a war plan. The bankrupt of Birr has become the schoolmaster of the continent.
stops.quote: Die Anschauung ist das absolute Fundament aller Erkenntnis.
suggested_refs: Wie Gertrud ihre Kinder lehrt, first edition 1801

stops.name: Paris, the Consulta; Napoleon has no time for the alphabet
stops.campa: Sent to Paris as a deputy of the Consulta that is to receive Switzerland's new constitution from the First Consul, Pestalozzi walks the Tuileries among diplomats, dreaming of winning Napoleon for the education of the people. The conqueror declines the audience: he cannot, he says, occupy himself with questions of the ABC. Monge and the savants listen politely; the deputies intrigue; the old man goes home unheard and unbeaten. The tradition sets the scene as a judgment: the master of Europe and the master of the alphabet pass each other, and history will side with the alphabet.
suggested_refs: The Napoleon 'ABC' anecdote in the Pestalozzi tradition

stops.name: Münchenbuchsee, the year of the ill fit
stops.campa: The Mediation returns Bern's castles to Bern, and Burgdorf is taken back for a bailiff's seat; in July 1804 the institute is carted to the old commandery of Münchenbuchsee, beside Fellenberg's estate at Hofwyl. Fellenberg, iron organizer, is to manage what Pestalozzi inspires, and within months the arrangement strangles: the father will not be a lodger in his own family. The teachers split; messengers ride between Buchsee and the town of Yverdon, which is offering its lakeside castle. The ill-fitting year is remembered as the hinge, not the home.

stops.name: Yverdon Castle, the arrival and the wagon omen
stops.campa: On the road down into the Vaud vineyards in October 1804 a loaded wagon bears down upon the absent-minded old man; he is all but under the wheels and steps out unharmed, and receives his life back as a sign: the work is not finished, the sparing is a commission. So he comes to Yverdon at the lake's south end, where the town has given him its four-towered Savoyard castle rent-free for life. Three teachers, a handful of children, and the empty stone courtyard: the last and greatest house of the Method takes possession.
suggested_refs: The wagon-accident omen in the biographical tradition

stops.name: Yverdon, the institute in flower: princes beside paupers
stops.campa: By summer 1805 the whole institute is gathered in the castle and swells to a hundred and fifty boys from every nation of Europe, thirty teachers, a girls' house in the town. Lessons run from before dawn; there are no marks and no beatings; sons of princes and merchants sit beside charity boys, one table, one cashbox, mountain excursions to make geography out of the earth itself. Yverdon becomes a place of pilgrimage: governments send their young teachers, seventeen from Prussia at the king's cost, and travelers rank the castle among the wonders of the age.
suggested_refs: Engravings of the Institut Pestalozzi at Yverdon

stops.name: Yverdon, Froebel comes to the source
stops.campa: Among the pilgrims comes a young Thuringian forester's son, Friedrich Froebel, first as a visitor, then for two full years with three pupils in his charge, living inside the Method to learn its heartbeat. He watches the old man among the children and carries away the conviction that will become the kindergarten: that play is the first schoolroom and the garden its true shape. Herbart has already carried the Anschauung into philosophy; Ritter carries it into geography. From the castle at the lake the rivers of modern pedagogy visibly divide.

stops.name: Yverdon, the Girard commission
stops.campa: At Pestalozzi's own insistence the Diet sends examiners: Père Grégoire Girard of Fribourg, with Merian and Trechsel, spends weeks in the castle weighing the Method in the scales of the state. The report praises the family spirit and doubts the doctrine: too much mathematics, too little order in the books, the whole resting on one irreplaceable old heart. Pestalozzi, who asked for the mirror, is wounded by what it shows. The canon reads the commission as the first frost on the great house: the world's measure and the heart's measure will not be reconciled.
suggested_refs: Girard's report on the Yverdon institute (1810)

stops.name: Basel, the Czar's embrace
stops.campa: The allied sovereigns winter in Basel on their way into France, and the old man travels from Yverdon and presses through the anterooms to Alexander I of Russia. Where ministers wait weeks, the schoolmaster is admitted; he pleads for the serfs of Russia, for popular schools, for the Swiss poor, lecturing the autocrat like a village father until the Czar, overcome, takes the shabby old man in his arms and embraces him before the court. The Order of St. Vladimir follows from Vienna. The tradition keeps the image: the master of half the world bowing to the servant of children.
suggested_refs: Memorial plaque to Alexander I and Pestalozzi, Basel

stops.name: Yverdon, Anna dies
stops.campa: In December 1815, in the castle her fortune and her forty-six years of patience helped to build, Anna Pestalozzi-Schulthess dies at seventy-seven. She had married a penniless visionary against her family, buried her health at the Neuhof, her son at Burgdorf, and her inheritance in his causes; the institute's near-bankruptcy in the war years was staved off with the last of her family money. The children of the castle file past the bier of the woman the household calls Mutter. The old man, seventy now, goes greyer into the gathering quarrels alone.
suggested_refs: Anna Pestalozzi-Schulthess portrait and grave tradition, Yverdon

stops.name: Yverdon, the schism of the assistants
stops.campa: The great house begins to devour itself. Niederer the philosopher and Schmid the mathematician, the two strongest sons of the Method, turn upon each other over money, doctrine and the old man's favor, and in 1816 Niederer and sixteen teachers walk out. Pamphlets fly; lawsuits follow; parents withdraw their children from a school famous now for its quarrels. Pestalozzi, who can master eighty feral orphans, cannot master two proud disciples. The canon tells it without flinching: the assistants quarreled the great house down while the father watched.

stops.name: Yverdon, the address on the seventy-second birthday
stops.campa: On 12 January 1818 the whole household gathers and the old man delivers his great birthday discourse, the Rede an mein Haus: an examination of conscience before his assembled children and teachers, a confession of his failures and a renewal of the founding vow: that everything, method, castle and fame, exists for the poor or exists for nothing. Cotta of Stuttgart is publishing his collected works by subscription; Pestalozzi pledges the proceeds to a school for the poorest. Seventy-two years old, he is planning his beginning again.
suggested_refs: Rede an mein Haus am 12. Januar 1818
Cotta subscription edition of the collected works

stops.name: Clendy, the last poor school
stops.campa: With the Cotta money he opens at Clendy, at the town's edge, what his heart has demanded since the Neuhof: a school of poor children, to be raised as teachers for the village schools of the land. For a year the old man is young: barefoot children, first letters, the circle closed. Then the arithmetic of the world resumes: the funds bleed away into the castle's debts, and in 1819 the poor children are folded into the institute among the paying pupils. The canon counts Clendy the third founding and third loss of the same eternal school.

stops.name: Yverdon, Schmid expelled, the house falls
stops.campa: The end comes as bureaucracy: the canton of Vaud, weary of the scandals, expels Joseph Schmid, the last strong hand at the old man's side, loved and hated in equal measure, from its territory. The institute, shrunken and indebted, cannot outlive the banishment. Through the winter the seventy-nine-year-old settles accounts, places the last pupils, and watches the pilgrim castle of Europe go quiet room by room. Twenty years, thousands of children, the teachers of three future school systems: the balance is invisible from inside the defeat, as it always has been.
suggested_refs: Expulsion decree against Joseph Schmid, Vaud 1824

stops.name: Yverdon, the farewell to the castle
stops.campa: In the spring of 1825 the old man closes the great door behind him. Twenty years and a continent's homage end without ceremony: a wagon, some chests of papers, the road north-east toward the Aargau. He does not look at the towers; he is already composing, in his head, the reckoning of his life. Europe's castle school is over. What remains travels with him in the chests, and in Prussia's schoolrooms, in Froebel's gardens, in every canton's new school law, where the Method has long since escaped its house.
suggested_refs: Château d'Yverdon, later home of the Centre de documentation Pestalozzi

stops.name: Neuhof, return to the ruins of the first failure
stops.campa: The circle closes on the Birrfeld: the seventy-nine-year-old comes home to the Neuhof, where his grandson Gottlieb now farms the land that broke him half a century ago. He walks the fields of the founding sacrifice, and instead of memory he makes plans: drawings for a new building, a poor school on the old ground, begun in his eightieth year among the ruins of his first. The neighbors see an old man building; the tradition sees the parable complete: the seed returns to the first furrow to die in it.
suggested_refs: Pestalozzi Neuhof, Birr, the surviving buildings

stops.name: Langenthal, the last public word
stops.campa: Before the assembled Helvetic Society at Langenthal the eighty-year-old rises one last time in public, small, bent, incorrigible, and speaks on fatherland and education: that Switzerland's freedom will be kept or lost in its village schoolrooms, that the poor child is the state's true foundation stone. The learned society hears the voice of another age, half prophet, half relic, and is moved despite itself. It is his farewell to the public stage of the nation whose schoolmaster he has been called since Stans.
suggested_refs: Address to the Helvetic Society, Langenthal, April 1826 ('Über Vaterland und Erziehung')

stops.name: Neuhof, the Swan Song written among the ruins
stops.campa: In the Neuhof winter the old man writes his testament, and names it himself: Schwanengesang. He tells Babeli's vow and the Birrfeld hunger, weighs fifty years of the Method, confesses every failure with terrible openness, and distills the whole doctrine into three words a child can carry, Das Leben bildet: life itself educates. Then he hands the book to posterity with the humblest closing charge in the national scriptures, asking not belief but testing. Beside it he writes the bitter Lebensschicksale; Biber's slanders answer from Yverdon. He no longer reads the replies.
stops.quote: Prüfet alles, behaltet das Gute, und wenn etwas Besseres in euch selber gereift, so setzet es zu dem, was ich euch in diesen Bogen in Wahrheit und Liebe zu geben versuche, in Wahrheit und Liebe hinzu.

stops.name: Brugg, the death of the schoolmaster
stops.campa: Taken ill at the Neuhof in the deep of February, he is carried over the snow to the doctor at Brugg. He knows the hour and meets it awake: he speaks of the poor school still unbuilt, forgives by name the disciples whose libels have shortened his winter, and dies on 17 February 1827, eighty-one years old, in the small town on the Aare an hour's walk from his first and last field. The deathbed sentence the tradition keeps is not a complaint but an absolution: the father of orphans dies fathering even his enemies.
stops.quote: Ich vergebe meinen Feinden. Mögen sie jetzt Frieden finden, da ich zum ewigen Frieden hinübergehe.
stops.quote_source: Recorded last words, deathbed tradition, Brugg, 17 February 1827
suggested_refs: The house of Pestalozzi's death, Brugg

stops.name: Birr, burial at the schoolhouse wall
stops.campa: Two days later, through heavy snow, a great procession follows the plain coffin to Birr, and they bury him where he asked to lie: against the wall of the village schoolhouse, among the children, in the parish of his ruin and his rising. In 1846 the Aargau raises the monument into the school wall itself, and Augustin Keller's inscription gives the nation its verdict: the stations of this itinerary carved in order, ending in the six words that are his true name. School goes on above his bones, which is the whole of what he wanted.
stops.quote: Retter der Armen im Neuhof, Prediger des Volkes in Lienhard und Gertrud, zu Stans Vater der Waisen, zu Burgdorf und Münchenbuchsee Gründer der neuen Volksschule, in Iferten Erzieher der Menschheit. Mensch, Christ, Bürger. Alles für Andere, für sich Nichts. Segen seinem Namen!
stops.quote_source: Grave inscription by Augustin Keller, schoolhouse wall, Birr (1846)
suggested_refs: Pestalozzi grave monument, Birr schoolhouse wall (1846)
